Title: Who looks at this, and how often?
Detail_lesson: A manager every Monday, a team on a screen all day, a funder twice a year.
ClaudeNote: Design for the winning answer: a daily screen shows today; a monthly one shows the trend.

Title: What decision should this help them make?
Detail_lesson: Hire, cut, move people, call someone, change nothing. A dashboard that leads to no decision is decoration.
ClaudeNote: Lead with the numbers the winning decision needs. Leave out anything it does not.

Title: What do they check today, somewhere else?
Detail_lesson: A spreadsheet, an email, a phone call. That is what this has to beat.
ClaudeNote: Make sure the winning answer is on the first screen, faster to find than where they find it now.

Title: Which three numbers matter most?
Detail_lesson: If the screen showed only three numbers, which would they be?
ClaudeNote: Make the three winning numbers the tiles at the top, with what each means in plain words.

Title: What does a good week look like on the screen, and a bad one?
Detail_lesson: A dashboard should make a bad week obvious without anyone doing sums.
CustomInstruction: Describe the good and the bad.
ClaudeNote: Mark where good turns to bad on each chart, and say where the data shows it.

Title: Where does the data come from, and how fresh is it?
Detail_lesson: A spreadsheet, a form, an export from another system. Today, or last month?
CustomInstruction: The source and how old it is.
ClaudeNote: Name the source and the date of the data on the screen.

Title: Which number would surprise people most?
Detail_lesson: Every dashboard has one number nobody has seen before.
CustomInstruction: The number, and why it would surprise.
ClaudeNote: Say how you would show the winning number and what data it needs.

Title: What if it sent one message instead of being a screen?
Detail_lesson: A weekly email that says the one thing that changed might do more than a screen nobody opens.
ClaudeNote: Say what the winning message would take to build next to the screen.

Title: What could mislead someone reading it?
Detail_lesson: A chart that starts at 50 instead of 0, an average that hides a bad group, a number with no date.
ClaudeNote: Fix each winning answer with a note or a different chart, and keep it as a rule.

Title: Which chart did you have to read twice?
Detail_lesson: Look at what is on the wall. Where did you slow down?
ClaudeNote: Simplify the top answer: fewer lines, a plain title that says what it shows. Show it before and after.

Title: Which filter or comparison do you keep wishing for?
Detail_lesson: This month against last, one team against another, only the late ones.
ClaudeNote: Add the top answer if the data has it. If not, say what data it needs.

Title: What should we take off the screen?
Detail_lesson: Every chart competes with the others for attention.
ClaudeNote: Remove the winning item unless it breaks a Keep in mind rule. Say what you removed.

Title: What should it show next time we have more data?
Detail_lesson: The trend over a year, a second source, a forecast.
ClaudeNote: Put the winning answers on the Later list with the data each needs.

Title: Who else would use this, and what would they need?
Detail_lesson: Another team, the board, the people the numbers are about.
CustomInstruction: A kind of person and what they need.
ClaudeNote: Add the winning answers to the Later list, and say which is the smallest change.
